topic: Day 2 · GI Bleeding on Antithrombotics — The Restart Dilemma
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Cardiovascular & Anticoagulation Service
speakerBio: Cardiologist who runs the joint anticoagulation-and-bleeding clinic and is on a personal crusade against the discharge summary that says only 'warfarin held'.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 72-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve, and on clopidogrel after a drug-eluting stent placed six weeks ago, arrives vomiting blood. His INR is 3.8, his systolic pressure is 88, and he is on his third unit of red cells. Two clocks are now ticking against you at once. Reverse him too hard and his valve thromboses or his fresh stent occludes; reverse him too little and he exsanguinates. And when the bleeding stops, the hardest question of the admission is still waiting: when do you turn the anticoagulation back on? Tonight is about holding your nerve on both clocks.

1 · ⚖️ The two-clock problem

Every antithrombotic-associated bleed is a collision between two competing risks, and good management is the art of not over-correcting either one:

Bleeding clockThrombotic clock
What it threatensExsanguination, shock, transfusion, rebleedStroke, valve thrombosis, stent thrombosis, VTE, MI
Driven byActive bleeding + degree of anticoagulationStrength of the original indication
Fast or slow?Fast — minutes to hoursSlow but lethal — hours to weeks off therapy
The errorUnder-reverse → the patient bleeds to deathOver-reverse / never restart → the patient clots to death
Stopping the bleeding is the emergency everyone sees. Restarting the anticoagulant is the emergency nobody sees — until the stroke.
💡 The under-taught truth

Across the literature on anticoagulant-associated GI bleeding, withholding anticoagulation causes more thromboembolic deaths than restarting causes fatal rebleeds. The reflex to "just leave the warfarin off to be safe" is one of the commonest and most lethal errors in this whole field. Safety in these patients is usually restarting, not abstaining.

2 · 🩸 Acute management — hold, resuscitate, reverse (selectively)

The immediate priorities are the same as any major GI bleed — ABC, two large-bore cannulae, restrictive transfusion to a haemoglobin threshold of ~70 g/L (higher, ~80, in active cardiac ischaemia), and urgent endoscopy after resuscitation. The antithrombotic-specific layer is: hold the drug, decide whether to actively reverse, and weigh the thrombotic cost of doing so.

  • Hold all antithrombotics at presentation.
  • Reverse actively only if bleeding is major/life-threatening — not for every raised INR. A stable ooze in a valve patient may need holding and endoscopy, not full reversal.
  • Endoscopic haemostasis is the definitive "reversal" — mechanical control of the lesion lets you get the anticoagulant back on sooner.

3 · 💉 Agent-by-agent reversal

Warfarin (vitamin-K antagonist)

For major bleeding: 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) 25–50 U/kg (dose by INR and weight) PLUS intravenous vitamin K 5–10 mg. PCC works in minutes by replacing factors II, VII, IX, X; vitamin K is slower (hours) but sustains the correction once PCC wears off — give both. PCC is preferred over FFP: faster, smaller volume, more reliable INR correction, less TACO. FFP only if PCC is unavailable.

DOACs (direct oral anticoagulants)

  • Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor) → idarucizumab 5 g IV — a specific monoclonal-fragment antidote, near-instant reversal (RE-VERSE AD).
  • Factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) → andexanet alfa where available and affordable (ANNEXA-4), or 4-factor PCC 50 U/kg as a pragmatic, widely-used alternative.
  • Check timing and renal function — a DOAC taken 20+ hours ago in a patient with normal renal function may already be largely cleared; the last-dose time and eGFR tell you how much drug is actually on board. Activated charcoal helps if the last dose was within ~2–4 hours.

Heparins

Protamine sulfate fully reverses unfractionated heparin (1 mg per ~100 units of heparin given in the preceding hours) and partially reverses low-molecular-weight heparin.

Antiplatelets

There is no true pharmacological reversal. Platelet transfusion is not routinely recommended in antiplatelet-associated bleeding (the PATCH trial showed harm in intracerebral haemorrhage) and should be reserved for life-threatening bleeding or before an emergency procedure. Time and holding the drug are the main "reversal."

AgentReversal / antidoteKey dose / caveat

4 · ☠️ The danger of over-correction

Reversal is not free. In the patient with a strong thrombotic indication, driving the INR to 1.0 and flooding them with clotting factors can precipitate the very catastrophe the anticoagulant was preventing.

⚠️ The patients where over-reversal kills

Mechanical heart valves (especially mitral, older-generation, or with AF) can thrombose within days of full reversal — valve thrombosis is often fatal. Very recent coronary stents (bare-metal <1 month, drug-eluting <3–6 months) can undergo acute stent thrombosis, which presents as a large MI with ~1-in-3 mortality. In these patients, reverse only as much as you must to stop life-threatening bleeding, get endoscopic control fast, and plan to re-anticoagulate early — often with a bridging heparin infusion you can switch off in seconds if bleeding recurs.

5 · 🔄 The RESTART decision — the heart of this lecture

Here is where most of the avoidable deaths hide, and where teaching is thinnest. Once haemostasis is achieved, the default is not "leave it off and see." The default is: anticoagulation should usually be restarted.

  • Why: Observational data across GI-bleed and warfarin cohorts consistently show that patients who resume anticoagulation after a GI bleed have lower mortality and lower thromboembolism, with only a modest increase in rebleeding — a net benefit. Never restarting is associated with the worst outcomes.
  • When: Timing balances rebleed risk (highest in the first ~72 h) against thrombotic risk. Most guidance and cohort data support restarting after roughly 3–7 days once haemostasis is secure — earlier for very high thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent stent, high-CHA₂DS₂-VASc AF, recent VTE), later only if the bleed was severe or the lesion is not yet controlled.
  • How: For warfarin/DOAC AF, resume the oral agent; for the highest thrombotic risk, a heparin bridge lets you restart cautiously with an off-switch. Consider switching to a DOAC (lower GI-bleed-fatality profile than warfarin for AF) and always fix the bleeding lesion and co-prescribe a PPI.
The question after a GI bleed is not "can I stop the anticoagulant?" — it is "when do I restart it?" For most patients the answer is days, not never.
🎯 Bleeding risk vs thrombotic risk — the contrast that decides timing

High thrombotic / lower rebleed (mechanical valve, stent <6 weeks, recent large VTE, controlled ulcer with clip + PPI) → restart early, consider bridging. High rebleed / lower thrombotic (uncontrolled or untreatable lesion, diffuse angioectasia, low-CHA₂DS₂-VASc AF) → delay, treat the lesion first, and consider whether the indication itself can be modified (e.g. left atrial appendage occlusion for AF that cannot tolerate anticoagulation).

6 · 💊 Aspirin for secondary prevention — do NOT stop it

A special and frequently mishandled case: the patient on low-dose aspirin for established cardiovascular disease (prior MI, stent, stroke) who bleeds. The instinct is to stop it. The evidence says keep it going.

  • In secondary prevention, continuing low-dose aspirin through a GI bleed carries a mortality benefit — stopping it roughly doubles major adverse cardiovascular events, and the excess cardiovascular deaths outweigh the rebleed risk.
  • A landmark RCT of aspirin-associated peptic-ulcer bleeding found that patients randomised to continue aspirin (with a PPI) had lower all-cause mortality than those who stopped it, at the cost of a small increase in (usually manageable) rebleeding.
  • Practical rule: for secondary-prevention aspirin, hold for at most a day or two around endoscopic haemostasis if you must, then resume promptly under PPI cover. Primary-prevention aspirin (no established vascular disease) can simply be stopped — its benefit is marginal.
⚠️ DAPT after recent PCI — do not casually drop the P2Y12 inhibitor

In dual antiplatelet therapy after a recent stent, stopping both agents risks acute stent thrombosis. Involve cardiology urgently. The usual compromise for a controlled bleed is to keep aspirin, hold the P2Y12 inhibitor for the shortest possible time, and resume it as soon as haemostasis allows — the shorter the interval since the stent, the more dangerous any interruption.

7 · 🛡️ PPI co-prescription — the enabler of restarting

A proton-pump inhibitor is the tool that makes restarting antithrombotics safe. Co-prescribed PPIs substantially reduce recurrent upper-GI bleeding in patients on aspirin, DAPT, or anticoagulants, and they are the reason "continue the aspirin" is a safe instruction. Every patient restarted on an antithrombotic after an upper-GI bleed — and every high-risk patient on DAPT or anticoagulant-plus-antiplatelet — should be on a PPI. Test and treat H. pylori as well (covered in session 16).

☠️ M&M — the stroke that came from stopping

A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5) and a prior TIA was admitted with a bleeding gastric ulcer on warfarin. Endoscopy achieved excellent haemostasis with a clip and adrenaline injection, and she was started on a high-dose PPI. Her warfarin was stopped — appropriately — during the acute bleed. But on discharge the summary read only "warfarin held," with no plan and no restart date. Her GP, seeing "held," left it off. Nine weeks later she returned with a dense left-MCA territory ischaemic stroke and died in a nursing home three months on. Her ulcer never rebled. Lessons: the anticoagulation decision does not end when the bleeding stops — it ends when a restart plan is written and owned. "Held" is not a plan; it is a time-bomb. In a patient with a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 5, the thrombotic clock was always the greater killer, and every guideline pointed to restarting within days once the clipped ulcer was secure. She died of the treatment we forgot to give back.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Two clocks: bleeding is fast and visible; thrombosis is slow, silent, and often the greater killer. Don't over-correct either.
  2. Reverse by agent: warfarin → 4F-PCC + IV vitamin K (both); dabigatran → idarucizumab; Xa inhibitors → andexanet or PCC; heparin → protamine; antiplatelets have no routine reversal (platelets can harm — PATCH).
  3. Reverse only for major bleeding, and beware over-reversal in mechanical valves and very recent stents — valve/stent thrombosis can be fatal.
  4. RESTART is the key decision: anticoagulation should usually be restarted after haemostasis — withholding it kills more patients by thromboembolism than restarting kills by rebleed.
  5. Timing: typically restart at ~3–7 days once haemostasis is secure; earlier (with a heparin bridge) for mechanical valves/recent stents/high-risk AF.
  6. Do NOT stop secondary-prevention aspirin — continuing it (with a PPI) saves lives; only primary-prevention aspirin can simply be stopped.
  7. Co-prescribe a PPI and test-and-treat H. pylori — this is what makes restarting safe. And never discharge with "held" and no plan.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on warfarin with a mechanical mitral valve has a major upper-GI bleed and an INR of 4. How do you reverse them, and what is the specific danger?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: For life-threatening bleeding I reverse with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 25–50 U/kg IV plus intravenous vitamin K 5–10 mg — PCC because it corrects the INR in minutes with a small volume and less TACO than FFP, and vitamin K because it sustains the correction once the PCC factors wear off. The specific danger is over-correction causing mechanical valve thrombosis, which can be fatal within days — a mitral prosthesis is especially high-risk. So I reverse only as far as I must to control life-threatening bleeding, prioritise rapid endoscopic haemostasis as the definitive control, and plan early re-anticoagulation, typically via a heparin infusion I can switch off instantly if bleeding recurs. I would not leave a mechanical-valve patient fully reversed and unbridged for long.

moderatorQs.q: Why is 'just leave the anticoagulant off to be safe' after a GI bleed often the wrong call?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because it treats only the risk you can see. Across GI-bleed and warfarin cohorts, patients who resume anticoagulation after haemostasis have lower mortality and fewer thromboembolic events, with only a modest rise in rebleeding — a clear net benefit — and never restarting is associated with the worst outcomes. Withholding anticoagulation causes more thromboembolic deaths (strokes, valve and stent thrombosis) than restarting causes fatal rebleeds. The correct framing after the bleeding stops is not 'can I stop it?' but 'when do I restart it?' — usually at around 3–7 days once haemostasis is secure, earlier for the highest thrombotic risk. 'Held indefinitely' is a decision that quietly kills.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on low-dose aspirin for a previous MI develops a bleeding peptic ulcer. Do you stop the aspirin?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — this is secondary-prevention aspirin and stopping it is dangerous. A landmark RCT of aspirin-associated ulcer bleeding showed that patients who continued aspirin with a PPI had lower all-cause mortality than those who stopped, at the cost of a small, usually manageable increase in rebleeding — because stopping roughly doubles major cardiovascular events and the excess cardiac deaths outweigh the bleeding. So I achieve endoscopic haemostasis, start a high-dose PPI, hold the aspirin for at most a day or two around the procedure if absolutely necessary, and resume it promptly. The exception is primary-prevention aspirin (no established vascular disease), which has marginal benefit and can simply be stopped.

audienceQs.q: Our patient took apixaban and we have no andexanet on the shelf. What can we actually give?
audienceQs.answerHTML: For life-threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor without andexanet alfa, give 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 50 U/kg — it is the widely-used pragmatic alternative and is what most UK protocols default to. First establish when the last dose was and the renal function: apixaban has a ~12-hour half-life, so a dose taken 20+ hours ago with normal eGFR may already be largely cleared and may need no reversal at all. If the last dose was within about 2–4 hours, add oral activated charcoal to limit further absorption. And remember the definitive control is endoscopic haemostasis — the PCC just buys you the window to get there.

audienceQs.q: Patient is on DAPT six weeks after a drug-eluting stent and is bleeding. How do I avoid stent thrombosis?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Six weeks post-DES is a high-risk window, and stopping both antiplatelets can precipitate acute stent thrombosis — a large MI with roughly 1-in-3 mortality. Involve cardiology immediately. The standard compromise for a controlled bleed is to keep the aspirin and hold the P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel/ticagrelor) for the shortest possible time, resuming it as soon as endoscopic haemostasis allows — often within days. Do not reflexively transfuse platelets to 'reverse' the antiplatelets: that is reserved for truly life-threatening bleeding and can promote stent thrombosis. Get definitive endoscopic control fast and cover with a high-dose PPI so you can get the P2Y12 inhibitor back on early.

audienceQs.q: How do I write the discharge plan so the anticoagulant actually gets restarted?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Never write just 'anticoagulant held' — that is how patients end up permanently off treatment and stroke. Write an explicit, owned restart plan: the drug and dose, the exact restart date (typically ~3–7 days after secure haemostasis, earlier for mechanical valves or recent stents), who is responsible (you, the GP, or anticoagulation clinic), the PPI co-prescription, and any H. pylori eradication and confirmation-of-cure plan. State the indication and its thrombotic risk (e.g. 'AF, CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5 — high stroke risk, restart apixaban on day 5 with PPI'). A named date and a named owner are what turn 'held' from a time-bomb into a safe pause.
